title: How to Measure the ROI of In-Store Promotions
summary: Learn how to measure in-store promotion ROI using incremental profit, shopper exposure, engagement, and sales data to evaluate promotion performance.
body_markdown:
Measuring the return on investment (ROI) of an in-store promotion means finding out whether the promotion earned more profit than it cost. Sales figures alone can’t answer that. They show what sold, but not how shoppers responded to the promotion or how much of the increase it actually caused.


A reliable answer takes three things: proof that shoppers saw and engaged with the promotion, a credible measure of incremental sales against a baseline or control, and the resulting profit after accounting for the full investment.


Attention is the starting point. Before a retailer can attribute sales lift to a display or offer, it needs to know whether the promotion captured enough shopper attention to have had an opportunity to influence a purchase.


This guide explains how to measure promotion ROI, which metrics matter, and how shopper behavior data can help retailers and brands evaluate promotion performance.


## What Is the ROI of an In-Store Promotion?


The ROI of an in-store promotion measures the financial return generated relative to the cost of running it. It helps retailers and brands determine whether the additional profit from a promotion justified the investment.


The formula is: **ROI = (Incremental profit − Promotion costs) ÷ Promotion costs × 100**


Incremental profit is the additional profit attributable to the promotion compared with what would likely have happened without it. Promotion costs may include displays, signage, setup labor, advertising, and other campaign expenses.


The distinction between incremental sales and total sales matters. Some shoppers would have purchased the product even without the promotion. Their purchases contribute to total sales during the campaign, but they don’t necessarily represent additional sales generated by the promotion.


Discounts also affect profitability. A promotion may increase unit sales while reducing profit per unit. Measuring ROI requires accounting for both effects, along with any sales shifted away from other products.


## 3 Main Reasons Why Sales Lift Alone Doesn’t Show ROI


Sales lift measures the increase in sales during a promotion compared with a baseline. It’s a useful starting point, but it doesn’t explain the full financial result.


### 1. Sales Lift Doesn’t Show How Much Demand Was Incremental


A promotion can increase unit sales without generating a proportional increase in profit. Some shoppers may have purchased the product anyway, while others may switch from a competing product or another item in the same category.


For example, a CPG brand can compare sales results with aisle traffic, promotion exposure, and shopper engagement data to better understand how customers responded to its pricing strategy. If a promotion primarily attracts shoppers who were already likely to buy, the brand may need to reconsider whether temporary discounts are the best approach.


### 2. Sales Data Doesn’t Show Whether Shoppers Saw the Promotion


A promotion may underperform because the offer wasn’t compelling. It may also underperform because shoppers didn’t encounter the display in the first place.


Sales figures alone can’t reliably distinguish between these situations. Exposure and engagement measurements add context by showing how many shoppers entered the promotion area and how many interacted with the display.


### 3. Sales Totals Don’t Explain Which Elements Worked


A promotion combines several factors, including price, signage, product placement, and display design. When sales change, the total alone doesn’t show which elements drove the result.


For example, a regional retailer may find that certain in-aisle displays disrupt shopper movement or receive less engagement than expected. Testing different display locations and layouts can help the retailer understand how placement affects shopper behavior before making broader changes.


## How to Measure the ROI of an In-Store Promotion


A consistent measurement process makes it easier to compare promotions and identify opportunities for improvement. The following six steps combine financial analysis with shopper behavior measurements:


### Step 1: Define the Promotion Zone


Identify the area where the promotion will run. This could be an end-cap display, fixture, or an area around promotional signage. Define which products, stores, and dates are included in the analysis. Keep the measurement area consistent throughout the campaign so results can be compared fairly.


For retailers evaluating several displays, define each zone separately. This makes it easier to identify differences in shopper exposure and engagement by location.


### Step 2: Establish a Baseline


A baseline estimates what sales and shopper behavior would look like without the promotion. It provides a reference point for evaluating changes during the campaign. Retailers can compare results with historical performance, similar stores not running the promotion, or—with VISION—shoppers in the same store and time period who did not engage with the display. This within-store comparison removes much of the variation between locations and can produce a larger pool of observations, helping teams reach a reliable read with fewer stores.


Because shoppers who engage with a display may differ from those who do not, account for factors that could affect the comparison, including:


- Seasonality and holidays
- Changes in product availability
- Other promotions running at the same time
- Differences in store traffic
- Changes in pricing or product placement


A baseline helps separate normal fluctuations from promotion-related changes. A comparable control group, when available, can strengthen the analysis by helping estimate what would have happened without the campaign.


### Step 3: Measure Exposure, Engagement, & Conversion


Sales figures explain the outcome. Shopper behavior data adds context about how customers interacted with the promotion.


Three metrics are particularly useful.


- **Exposure** measures how many shoppers entered the area where the promotion was displayed. A display positioned away from common shopper routes may receive less exposure than one placed along a frequently used path.[Shopper path data](https://standard.ai/blog/shopper-path-data-store-layout/) can help retailers understand how customers move through the store and reach different displays.


Storewide[retail traffic analytics](https://standard.ai/blog/retail-traffic-analytics/) provides a broader view of traffic, while zone-level measurements help assess how many shoppers had an opportunity to encounter a specific promotion.


- **Engagement** measures how shoppers respond after entering the promotion zone. Depending on the setup, this may include stopping near a display or spending a defined amount of time in the area.[Dwell time in retail](https://standard.ai/blog/what-is-dwell-time-in-retail/) can provide additional context, although a longer stop doesn’t necessarily indicate purchase intent. Shoppers may also pause because they’re comparing products, waiting for assistance, or navigating a crowded aisle.
- **Conversion** measures the share of exposed or engaged shoppers who purchase the promoted product. The denominator should be defined consistently, depending on the question being evaluated.


Conversion analysis requires purchase data that can be matched to shopper activity by an appropriate time period and store area. A shopper stopping near a display doesn’t, by itself, establish that the display caused a purchase.


[Computer vision in retail](https://standard.ai/blog/computer-vision-in-retail/) can turn footage from existing store cameras into anonymous movement and behavior data without facial recognition. When combined with suitable sales data, these measurements can help retailers and brands assess how promotion exposure and engagement relate to purchasing outcomes.


For digital screens and other forms of[in-store retail media](https://standard.ai/blog/vision-transforms-in-store-retail-media/) , the same measurement principles apply: assess who had an opportunity to see the promotion, how shoppers responded, and how those observations relate to sales.


### Step 4: Estimate Incremental Sales


Compare sales during the promotion with the baseline to estimate the change in unit sales.


**Incremental unit sales = Actual sales during promotion − Estimated baseline sales**


For example, if a product typically sells 1,000 units during a comparable period and sells 2,500 units during the promotion, the observed increase is 1,500 units.


That increase isn’t automatically proof that the promotion generated 1,500 additional purchases. Other factors may have influenced sales, and shoppers may have switched from other products in the same category.


Check sales across the wider category to identify potential cannibalization. If the promoted product gains sales while neighboring products lose sales, some of the increase may reflect a shift in purchasing rather than additional category demand.


Where possible, use comparable stores or other suitable methods to estimate how much of the change was attributable to the promotion.


### Step 5: Calculate Incremental Profit & ROI


Once you’ve estimated incremental sales, calculate the financial impact of the promotion.


You’ll need:


- The regular selling price and product cost
- The promotional selling price and product cost
- Baseline and promotional sales
- Any estimated profit lost from neighboring products
- The total cost of running the promotion


Use these calculations as a starting point:


- **Regular profit per unit** = Regular selling price − Product cost
- **Promotional profit per unit** = Promotional selling price − Product cost
- **Incremental profit** = Promotional-period profit − Baseline profit − Estimated profit lost on other products
- **Profit after promotion costs** = Incremental profit − Promotion costs
- **ROI** = Profit after promotion costs ÷ Promotion costs × 100


The calculation should use comparable periods and account for the discount across all units sold at the promotional price, including units that may have sold without the offer.


Supplier funding and other reimbursements should also be accounted for consistently. Depending on the retailer’s accounting approach, these may reduce the promotion’s effective cost.


### Step 6: Test Changes & Measure Again


Promotion measurement is more useful when retailers apply the findings to future campaigns. Change one element at a time where practical. For example, move a display to a different location, revise the signage, or test another offer. Then compare exposure, engagement, sales, and profitability against a suitable baseline.


Over multiple campaigns, these comparisons can help retailers identify which combinations of placement, messaging, and offers are associated with stronger results.


## A Worked Example of Promotion ROI


Consider a hypothetical promotion for a product with a regular selling price of $10 and a product cost of $6; its regular profit is $4 per unit.


During the promotion, the selling price drops to $8, reducing profit to $2 per unit. The promotion runs on an end-cap display, and the baseline comes from a comparable period.


The following figures are illustrative assumptions, in which each buyer is assumed to purchase one unit.


### What Shoppers Did in the Promotion Zone


Metric Baseline Promotion


Shoppers entering the zone 10,000 10,000


Shoppers who stopped 2,500 5,000


Units sold 1,000 2,500


Engagement rate 25% 50%


Purchase rate among engaged shoppers 40% 50%


Exposure remained unchanged at 10,000 shoppers. Engagement increased from 25% to 50%, and the share of engaged shoppers who purchased rose from 40% to 50%.


These figures suggest that more shoppers stopped at the display and purchased during the promotion. However, behavioral measurements alone don’t show how many purchases the promotion caused. The financial analysis provides a separate view of the result.


### What the Promotion Earned


Using the example’s assumed figures:


Calculation Amount


Baseline profit: 1,000 units × $4 $4,000


Promotion profit: 2,500 units × $2 $5,000


Estimated profit lost on neighboring products −$300


Incremental profit $700


Promotion costs −$500


Profit after promotion costs $200


ROI 40%


**The ROI calculation is: ($700 − $500) ÷ $500 × 100 = 40%**


Unit sales increased by 150%, but the promotion’s incremental profit was $700 before campaign costs, after accounting for the assumed loss on neighboring products.


The discount also affected the result. The 1,000 units that formed the baseline earned $2 less per unit at the promotional price, representing $2,000 in reduced profit compared with selling those units at the regular price. The additional 1,500 units generated $3,000 in profit at $2 per unit, before accounting for the estimated loss on neighboring products.


This is why a large sales increase doesn’t necessarily translate into an equally large financial return. Retailers need to consider pricing, baseline demand, other product sales, and campaign costs together.


## 6 Mistakes That Can Distort In-Store Promotion ROI


Even with the right metrics, several common mistakes can lead to misleading conclusions.


1. **Skipping the baseline.** Without a reasonable estimate of expected sales, normal changes in demand may be attributed to the promotion.
2. **Ignoring cannibalization.** A promoted product may gain sales at the expense of other products in the same category. Looking only at the promoted item can overstate the financial impact.
3. **Underestimating the effect of discounts.** The lower margin applies to all units sold at the promotional price, including purchases that may have occurred anyway.
4. **Overlooking stock availability.** A promoted product that runs[out of stock may miss potential sales](https://standard.ai/blog/hidden-cost-of-out-of-stocks-behavioral-data/) . Shoppers may leave without purchasing or choose another item.
5. **Counting employees as shoppers.** Staff movement near a display can inflate exposure measurements. Anonymous staff-exclusion methods, where supported, help keep shopper counts more accurate without facial recognition.
6. **Judging results too early.** A short measurement window may be affected by holidays, temporary traffic changes, or other promotions. Shoppers may also stock up during a promotion and buy less afterward, so check sales in the weeks that follow. Use a period long enough to evaluate results against comparable conditions.


## Measure More Than Sales Lift


Sales lift is a useful indicator of how a promotion performed, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Retailers also need to understand the cost of the offer, estimate how much additional profit it generated, and account for other factors that influenced the result.


Shopper behavior data adds another layer to that analysis. Exposure and engagement measurements help explain how customers interacted with a promotion, while sales and financial data show how those interactions relate to purchasing outcomes.


Together, these sources give retailers and brands a stronger basis for comparing promotions, evaluating performance, and deciding what to test next.
